A brief for Women Applying AI leadership

WAAI Engine Lab: How It Works

The Lab is a working product studio with a solid framework + methodology that doubles as curriculum.

Prepared by Jade Davila Date September 2026 Companion WAAI Engine Lab: Market Analysis

The High Level

Key elements in the framework that keep the engine running smoothly.

A dual-purpose framework

The Lab builds the products WAAI needs, and it teaches members to build their own. Both run on the same framework, the same review structure, and the same quality checks, so what a member learns on a WAAI product she takes to her own.

A human checks every piece of work

Every piece of work carries a check a human performs before it is accepted. Nothing ships to members until a release checklist is signed. This, accompanied by the framework, is the Lab's answer to 'AI slop'.

5-8 hours a week

One critique session a week, everything recorded, a showcase at every gate instead of a competition. Built for members with jobs, families, and businesses.

Members teach each other

Skill Swap runs inside the Lab. Each member names a skill she offers and one she seeks, and the Lab matches them and records who gave what. WAAI's exchange model is piloted here first.

The framework

Three parts sit at the center of every project. Around them runs a ten stage journey and a catalog of the work each stage requires.

The Product North Star

The product thesis: who it is for, what it must do, and what design moves are off limits, written specifically enough that even an AI agent can tell when a decision violates it.

No project opens a code editor without one.

The Council

Nine voices, each reading the work through one lens. Members are the voices in reviews, and AI critics run the same lenses continuously. The Council surfaces tensions rather than voting on them.

Critique is structured, expected, and safe.

The Foundation

Living documentation every person and every agent reads before touching the codebase and updates before leaving it. A pre push hook makes the workflow binding.

The handoff document is always current.

The Journey

Ten stages from Discovery to Scale. Each has a question, a definition of done, and the Council voices that lead it. A gate at the end of each stage is a Council review held to the North Star.

The Activity Catalog

Eighty nine activities across the ten stages. Each names who drives (human or AI), what AI can carry, what a human must own, and how the human knows it was done right.

The Council

Nine voices. Each one is also a seat on a project team and a Council guild across the Lab.

The stages are a loop. Learn feeds Iterate, Iterate feeds Build, and every stage is held to the North Star. A product lives for as long as the community needs it.

How to read the stages

Every stage is made of activities, and every activity is verified

Open any stage above and you will see its work broken into activities from the catalog. Each one carries a mode that says who drives, a set of suggested tools, and a check a human confirms before the work is accepted. 'AI slop' is accepting output you have not verified and could not explain; the check is what prevents it. Tools are the Lab's defaults, reviewed yearly and evaluated by each team before committing.

The four modes

  • human-onlyAI does not take part in the core act. Interviewing a user. Watching someone use the product. Making the call.
  • human-leadsThe human does the work, with AI helping on drafts, options, and drudgery.
  • human-ai-collaborateReal back and forth. Neither could do it as well alone.
  • ai-leadsAI does the work end to end. The human writes the spec, reviews the output, and verifies it against the check before accepting it.

A human is responsible for every activity in every mode. Whoever drives, the human still has to confirm the work passed its check.

ExampleWriting testsOne of the 89 activities, shown the way it appears inside a stage. Stage 5, Build.
Mode
ai-leads AI writes the tests. The human decides what to cover and reviews what was written.
Lab role
The Groundskeeper: QA engineer or software engineer
AI can do
Generate cases, write unit and integration tests, find untested paths
Human must own
What gets covered, the critical business logic tests, test quality over time
Pitfalls
Tests coupled to implementation; tests the human cannot say the purpose of; tests that pass because the expected values were pasted from the output
Tools
Vitest; Playwright; React Testing Library; Claude Code
Done right when
You can say what each test proves, the tests test behavior rather than implementation, nothing is hard coded to pass, and a deliberately introduced bug fails the suite.

At the end of the Journey: the release checklist

Nothing ships to members until every item is true and the Lab Lead has signed. This is the Lab's definition of great, made checkable.

  1. The North Star exists, is current, and the product is recognizably itself against it
  2. Every stage gate was held and its tensions are recorded
  3. The Foundation is current and the pre push hook has never been bypassed
  4. Tests and evals pass, and a deliberately broken release was blocked at least once
  5. Accessibility audit complete; an assistive technology user completed the core task
  6. Privacy review signed by whoever holds that responsibility for WAAI
  7. AI surfaces red teamed, with the attack list and fixes recorded
  8. A beta with real members happened, and at least one thing changed because of it
  9. Monitoring, alerting, and a runbook exist, and a named person receives the alerts
  10. A maintainer is named for after launch, and a succession plan exists

Two kinds of build

Org builds are linear by design. A named team holds the nine Council seats, every gate is held in order, and the product ships through the release checklist.

How a team works

A Lab team takes a WAAI product through the Journey gate by gate. Builders commit to a product through its next gate, and the team can change shape at a gate. Every gate ends with a showcase where the community sees what is real.

5 to 8

hours a week for a Builder, including the Council session. The work is sized to the hours available, never the reverse.

1

Council session per team per week, plus a short async check in. The heartbeat of the Lab and the main place learning happens.

All

synchronous rituals are recorded and have an async path. Sessions are scheduled in each team's own time zone overlap.

0

rankings. A showcase at every gate, public, where real members try the work. Judges are not part of it.

An example project

Every project is different, and the stage timelines will take shape accordingly. This is one example of how the ten stages might lay out over about eight months, with a Council gate at the end of each and the continuous activities running on. The stages overlap on purpose.

The gate is the unit of progress.

A team works toward the next gate, and a gate is a Council review held to the stage's definition of done. Reaching it is the only deadline that matters.

Stages overlap on purpose.

Validation starts while Discovery is still listening. Harden begins while Build is still shipping increments. Waiting for one stage to fully close before the next opens is how months get lost.

Every gate ends with a showcase.

The community sees what is real, real members try it, and nobody ranks anything. Launch is simply the showcase where the product goes live.

Teams change shape at gates.

Builders commit through the next gate. Seats can change hands there, shadows can step up, and the Foundation carries the knowledge across.

Continuous activities never end.

Security posture and cost awareness begin at Architecture. Monitoring and intelligence health begin at Build. Maintenance and support begin at Launch. They run for as long as the product lives.

Scale is open ended.

It begins when the product needs it and has no gate of its own. A product in Scale still runs the loop: Learn, Iterate, Build, at a lighter cadence.

Roles on an org build

The Council voices are the roster. Every project needs every voice heard, so someone takes each seat. With two or three members per voice across the Lab, no seat depends on one person.

Lab Lead

Owns the framework, the program, the roster, and the release checklist. Signs releases. Coaches project leads and runs the Council guild leads. Succession is a leadership decision.

Project lead

One per product. Owns the North Star and the decision at every gate. Holds the product to its North Star when the Council disagrees. Drawn from Builders who have taken a product through at least one gate.

Council seat holders

Nine seats per project, filled by Builders. Seats can double up on a small team, and a member of the relevant Council guild can hold a seat on a team she is not otherwise on.

Council guilds and their leads

A Council guild is everyone across the Lab who holds the same seat, so nine guilds, one per voice. They meet monthly to share what the seat is learning, grow members into seats they have not held, fill empty seats on projects, and host Skill Swap. Each has a guild lead, an experienced practitioner who coaches seat holders and reviews checks in that discipline. The guild leads are the Lab's mentor layer.

Shadows

New recruits who observe a seat through a gate before holding one. Where the next seat holders come from.

Observers

Everyone else. No obligations. Counted, welcomed, and periodically asked what would make them take a seat.

Member builds are not linear. Members arrive with products at every stage, from a napkin idea to something already launched. So the education track has a prerequisite walk through, then a way for a member to slot herself into the Journey wherever her product is, get help from the Council seats that lead that stage, and give help in the Councils where her own strengths lie.

First, the walk through

Before a member enters the program she completes Foundations: a self paced walk through the nine Councils and the ten stages, so she knows what it takes to build and launch a product that holds up. Each module follows the same loop: read the stage and its voice from the framework, watch a recorded Council session and a build-along from that stage, and do one activity from the catalog on her own idea, with its acceptance check as a guide. Foundations is open to every WAAI member, and a live cohort starts each month for anyone who wants company through it.

Then, slot in

Name her Councils

She names her primary Council, the one that is her wheelhouse, and if she has one, a secondary Council where she also has skills. These are what she offers. Everything she learns from the other Councils is what she receives in exchange.

Find her stage

Her product is somewhere on the ring. She names the stage honestly, using the definition of done for the stage before it. A product with no North Star is in Discovery whatever it looks like.

Ask that stage's Council

Every stage names the voices that lead it. She brings her work to those seats: the AI Council any time, the monthly open Council session for human critique, office hours, and the Council guild sessions where the people holding that seat gather.

Give from her Councils

She offers her expertise where she named it, through Skill Swap. The clinical director sits with The Long Game on someone else's compliance question; the marketer sits with The Merchant. Giving is how the track stays a community, and it is what pays for what she learns.

What she leaves with

A shipped product she owns outright, and a build log: her North Star, her artifacts, the seats she has held, and what she has taught and received. The build log is the evidence behind Foundations certification, which is earned by artifacts and shareable on LinkedIn, and later it is what she shows an investor. Members who go on to hold seats on Lab teams work toward Practitioner certification the same way.

For every member, whichever kind of build

Three ways in

Every member can take part at a level that fits her life right now, and move between levels.

Observer

Open to any member. No application. Sit in on any Council session, showcase, or Council guild meeting. Read every project's North Star. Invited to speak, with no expectation that she will.

To enter
Be a WAAI member.
First contributions
Discovery interviews, prototype tests, the member beta. Real work the Lab cannot do without real members.

Builder

Take a seat on a Lab project team and commit through its next gate. Hold a Council voice and belong to its Council guild.

To enter
One completed activity from the catalog with its check passed, reviewed by a Council guild lead, or the Foundations course.
Leads to
Project lead after a product has passed a gate with her in a seat. Practitioner certification after two seats held.

Solo founder

Build your own product using the framework. The AI Council stands in for the human one. Bring work to a monthly open Council session for human critique.

To enter
The Foundations course.
Owns
Everything she builds. WAAI claims nothing.

Skill Swap

Members are experienced professionals. The curriculum is each other. Six principles govern how the exchange runs inside the Lab.

The trade sets its own value

No formula, no rate card, no unit of account. If a surgeon agrees to give an hour of her expertise for help organizing her research lab, that trade is worth it to her, and that is the end of the question. Longer-term exchanges or partnerships may be negotiated individually among members.

Square is a complete outcome

A one time exchange, finished and acknowledged, is full and final payment. Nothing is owed and nothing is tracked forward.

Giving back is a first class mode

Some members will give time or expertise without seeking anything. Gifts are recorded as gifts and made visible. The receiver owes nothing.

Trades are rarely one to one

The person a member helps often cannot give her what she needs. The Lab closes loops across the community, and software does the matching so nobody does the accounting by hand.

Being a user is real work

Interviews, prototype tests, and betas are contributions the Lab cannot complete without real members. A newcomer has this to offer immediately, and it counts.

The record makes work visible

The purpose of recording who gave what is that invisible, uncompensated work becomes visible and credited. It is a record of contribution.

The Lab builds its own exchange

The member app prototype already has the offer and seek fields and a first matcher. The loop proposal, the record, and the nudges are the next product on the Lab roster.

When an exchange stops being a one off and a member's steady contribution helps another member's venture reach Launch and earn, the relationship can convert to something with a claim attached. The exchange value system is a work in progress. Anything past square trades is a question for counsel before it is a design question.

How it starts

A phased start, so the program is tested before it is announced at scale.

  1. Approval and setupThis monthLeadership approves the framework and the program shape. Legal review of the participation agreement. First Council guild leads recruited.
  2. PilotFirst product through its first gatesOne or two products, including the member app. Eight to twelve Builders. Observers open to everyone. The Lab Lead logs what the framework and program get wrong.
  3. Foundations courseAfter the pilotBuilt from the pilot's learnings and its recordings. First live cohort starts the following month.
  4. Open roster and publishOnce the pilot has launchedIntake opens to all members. Council guilds fully staffed. Practitioner track launches. The framework and the Lab's results are published.

Decisions for leadership

What this brief asks of you.

  1. Approve the framework and the program shape for a pilot, using the member app as the first product.
  2. Commission legal review of the participation agreement: the training framing, and the two ownership defaults (WAAI owns Lab products; members own their own).
  3. Confirm who at WAAI holds privacy responsibility and will sign releases.
  4. Approve the framework license (the author retains ownership, WAAI holds a perpetual license for the Lab and the course, and the framework is published under Creative Commons with attribution) and choose the framework's public name.
  5. Choose which partner conversations to open first.
  6. Weigh in on the open question: can WAAI help fund founder businesses that come through the Lab?
